pes.title: Combat Training Centers Support
pes.description: The Combat Training Centers (CTCs) are the Army's premiere collective training centers. The CTCs provide high-fidelity Live, Virtual and Constructive (LVC) Brigade training rotations which prepare Brigade Combat Teams, Joint partners, and supporting units to deploy in support of the Army's Sustainable Readiness Model (SRM). The CTC program supports the National Training Center (NTC), the Joint Readiness Training Center (JRTC), and the Joint Multinational Readiness Center (JMRC). The CTCs develop agile and adaptive leaders at the tactical, operational and strategic levels while providing BCTs the core training necessary to conduct decisive action in a dynamic operating environment. The Combat Training Center Instrumentation System (CTC-IS) is a communications, analysis and feedback system that provides a realistic operational environment for training the Brigade Combat Team (BCT) and below in preparation for deployment to conduct Unified Land Operations (ULO). It is comprised of voice, video, and data instrumentation subsystem networks that include software, hardware, work stations, base-station equipment, communications infrastructure, voice radios, data devices, and interfaces. The Instrumentation System provides the CTC Operations Group critical situational awareness for training safety, analysis, and feedback capabilities to conduct After Action Reviews (AARs). The Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center-Instrumentation System (JPMRC-IS) is a transportable instrumentation system that provides instrumented training for the Brigade Combat Team and below. JPMRC-IS is a rapidly deployable, self-supported system providing Observer Controller Communications, Battle Command, Soldier worn Instrumentation, Embedded Constructive Simulations, Training Analysis and Feedback (TAF) workstations, Voice and Video Monitoring, After Action Review (AAR) presentation, and its own power generation. JPMRC-IS performs the end-to-end mission functions of Exercise Planning, System Preparation, Exercise Management, Monitoring and Control, and Training Performance Feedback through onsite AARs and unit Take Home Packages. Training Aircraft Survivability Equipment (ASE) Stimulation Suite (TASS) is a live training system that utilizes Aircraft Survivability Equipment B-Kit Emulator (ABE) software application to support the need for units to replicate the Operational Environment (OE) at Maneuver Combat Training Center (MCTC) requirement. TASS supports U.S. Army helicopters during force-on-force exercises in the live training environment of the maneuver Combat Training Center (CTC). TASS consist of airborne and ground transceivers that exchange position and engagement data between the Aircraft Survivability Equipment (ASE) simulation, Ground Threat Emitters (GTE), and the CTC Instrumentation System (IS). Aircrafts use tracking and engagement data collected by the CTC- IS and is displayed as training performance feedback in an AAR. Threat Integrated Air Defense System (T

llm.summary: Supports the Army Combat Training Centers (NTC, JRTC, JMRC) by procuring instrumentation systems (CTC-IS, JPMRC-IS) and live training systems such as TASS for brigade-level live/virtual/constructive training.

pes.title: Surface Power Equipment
pes.description: Surface Power Equipment budget line provides life-cycle support for the following Marine Gas Turbine systems: The General Electric LM2500 Marine Gas Turbine provides main propulsion for the Navy's surface combatants including the CG 47 TICONDEROGA Class, DDG 51 ARLEIGH BURKE Class, and LCS-2 (Austal) Class. The LM2500 is composed of two major sub-assemblies: the gas generator and power turbine sections. It is coupled to the ship drive-train by a high speed coupling shaft. The LM2500+ Marine Gas Turbine and its associated Engineering Control Systems provide main propulsion power for the Navy's amphibious assault ships including the LHD-8 USS MAKIN ISLAND, LHA-6 USS AMERICA and LHA-7 USS TRIPOLI. The LM2500+ is composed of two major sub-assemblies: the gas generator and power turbine sections. It is coupled to the ship drive-train by a high speed coupling shaft. The control system for both engines provides for both local and remote engine operations. The Rolls Royce (Allison) 501-K Series Gas Turbines are used to drive electrical generators in Ship Service Gas Turbine Generators (SSGTG). The 501-K17 is used on the CG-47 Class ships. The 501-K34 is an upgraded version used on the DDG-51 Class ships and is not interchangeable with the 501-K17. The MT5S is a higher-power derivative of the 501-K engine family (utilizing Rolls Royce's new "Marine Trent" or "MT" naming convention vice the older "501-K" naming convention) used for auxiliary electrical generation on DDG-1000 class ships; the MT5S is not interchangeable with the 501-K17 or 501-K34. The MT5S is used within the RR4500 auxiliary turbine generator (ATG) aboard DDG-1000 Class ships. The MT5S-HE+ is used within the AG9160RF SSGTG aboard DDG-51 Flight III ships. Based on the MT5S design, the MT5S-HE+ includes several material changes designed to improve fuel efficiency and increase AG9160RF electrical power output when compared to the RR4500. The Rolls Royce MT-30 is used on LCS-1 (Lockheed) Class for main propulsion and DDG 1000 for electrical generation. Rolls Royce 250-KS4 is used as a starter gas turbine for the 501-K34 on DDG 79 and follow. The Rolls Royce MT7 gas turbine is used for both lift and propulsion fan power on the next generation of LCAC landing craft. Digital Fuel Control (DFC) procurement quantities are based upon the DDG modernization schedule and quantities are procured one year in advance of the scheduled availabilities due to long material lead times. The Surface Power Equipment budget line may also be used to procure spare waterborne shafting (propeller shafts and stern tube shafts) and controllable pitch propeller (CPP) system end items such as propeller blades, hubs and oil distribution (OD) boxes used on DDG 51 class ships. pes.title: Surface Combatant HM&E
pes.description: This program allows the Navy to better align and identify Hull, Mechanical & Electrical (HM&E) requirements and shipboard upgrades and equipment. This is in support of the in-service Surface Combatants and Amphibious ships to include Class Common Equipment (CCE) to support shorter Regular Overhauls and Selected Restricted Availabilities. These include Ship System Components that require long repair turn-around; CG/DDG - Machinery Control Systems (MCS) Commercial off the Shelf (COTS) Refresh; Ship Control Systems (SCS) procurements and installation in support of the SCS; and other equipment to support the Comprehensive Review Findings following the Fitzgerald and McCain collisions in 2017. [P40A / GB001 - CG/DDG COTS Tech Refresh]: Due to Diminishing Manufacturing Sources and Material Shortages (DMSMS), Commercial Off The Shelf (COTS) equipment must be periodically refreshed to ensure supportability to the Fleet. This cost code is used to fund solutions for HM&E systems that have parts with impending DMSMS impacts. DMSMS solutions, including after-market manufacturing (reverse engineering), bridge-buys, life-of-type buys, modernization through replacement, modification / redesign, and reclamation are implemented to ensure that in-service ships are operational and sustainable throughout the life of the system. DMSMS issues and planned resolutions are implemented both within and outside of standard CNO availabilities (Window of Opportunity (WOO) or Continuous Maintenance Availability (CMAV)) and are impacted by pending fact-of-life influences, including shifting availabilities, modified vendor End of Sale dates, and unforeseen material shortages. [P40A / GB002 - Class Common Equipment]: The Common Class Equipment (CCE) program is to provide Ready-For-Issue (RFI) systems and equipment in support of Surface Combatant ship industrial availabilities and to replace major system equipment which sustains battle damage or major failure. CCE Availability Assets (AAs) ensure warfighting capability, readiness, and on-time deployment by providing RFI long lead time material (LLTM) in case of possible catastrophic damage or major failure on Aegis ships. CCE AAs are procured and stored to support backfit upgrades and emergent maintenance within brief availability windows. The ready accessibility of these assets avoids delays in availability completion caused by lengthy equipment repair turn-around time or acquisition lead time. In addition to AAs, the CCE program also provides for Insurance Assets. These are the major long lead time HM&E equipment/systems, which would prevent a ship from being able to be quickly repaired in order to accomplish its mission due to major damage or battle damage. The CCE program provides for both CG and DDG assets. [P40A / GB003 - Ship Control Systems (Surface Ship Modernization)]: Funds provide support for the procurement and installation of Ship Control Systems (SCS) upgrades on both cruisers and destroyers in support of the Fleet

pes.title: Other Navigation Equipment
pes.description: This program provides procurement and improvements of navigation equipment to include Inertial Navigation equipment such as gyrocompasses, speed sensors, Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) and major components for other navigation systems. ECDIS provides Fleet-wide electronic charting capability, increases navigation and situational awareness, improves safety at sea, and eliminates reliance on paper charts. These systems provide mission critical navigation data to shipboard combat and weapon systems. [P40A / GW054: NAVIGATION TRAINING EQUIPMENT]: Funds are required for the procurement of training equipment for multiple Navigation classrooms in support of Navigation System Technician pipeline maintenance training and ECDIS Operator Training. This includes computer upgrades and software licenses. These upgrades are critical to maintaining Fleet proficiency on operation and maintenance of navigation systems. pes.title: Sub Periscope, Imaging and Supt Equip Prog
pes.description: The Submarine Periscope, Imaging, and Support Equipment program provides critical electromagnetic systems to all classes of submarine platforms. This includes Imaging, Electronic Warfare (EW), and RADAR systems which provide navigation safety and collision avoidance, particularly in high intensity littoral operations so that surveillance and weapons systems can be effectively employed. Integrated Submarine Imaging System (ISIS) and EW BLQ-10 systems are part of the Submarine Warfare Federated Tactical Systems (SWFTS), a family of interdependent systems that conduct cooperative system development, procurement, and installations. PMS435 procures and installs ISIS and EW BLQ-10 Technical Insertion (TI) shipsets, along with the other SWFTS Participating Acquisition Resource Managers (PARMs), PMS401 (A-RCI) under BLI 2150 and PMS425 (BYG-1) under BLI 5420. SWFTS TI shipsets must be procured and installed in like quantities (except EW SSBN (OHIO)) across all PARMs to maintain the SWFTS model. The Submarine Periscopes and Imaging Equipment Program procures ISIS including Type 18 and Type 8 periscope upgrades; the Photonics Mast and its variants, including the Type 20 and Type 24; inboard hardware kits; imaging upgrades for all submarine classes; Photonics land-based spares, depot tooling and mast maintenance equipment. ISIS supports high intensity operations in the littorals, providing the submarine force with the tactical imaging systems necessary to safely and effectively employ its surveillance and weapons capabilities. The infrared imaging capability provided by ISIS provides all weather imaging capability, improving imaging at night and in low visibility conditions. Technology Insertion initiatives include the common control and displays hardware and software on all platforms regardless of imaging sensors, an integrated imaging system that provides for operator alerts, imaging enhancement tools and contact analysis tools, incorporation of Type 20 Mast, Type 24 Mast, future sensors, and a fully Submarine Warfare Federated Tactical System (SWFTS) integrated system. Funding improves submarine imaging capability in the areas of: ship safety, Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR), and tactical control (contact management in the littorals) by providing high quality imaging 24 hours a day, 7 days a week in all weather conditions to support submarine operations worldwide. By OPNAV Ltr Ser. An ISIS Capability Development Document (CDD) was approved 22 Dec 2011, with an update to the CDD approved on 15 Mar 2018 and a CDD Annex for Low Profile Digital Photonics Mast approved on 02 Dec 2019. pes.title: Command and Control Switchboard
pes.description: The switchboard program provides mission critical switching capability required to link shipboard combat equipment including weapons, launchers, sensors, computers and navigation equipment. In essence, switchboards serve as the central connection point for most elements of combat and weapon systems, interior communications, data transfer, and command and control systems. They are designed to accommodate either analog, digital interfaces, or a combination of both. In total, this budget item supports approximately 200 ships and 1,000 pieces of equipment throughout the acquisition life cycle. Functions include: data routing, action cutout, test and operating mode selection (including casualty back-up modes), power monitoring and control, circuit protection, peripheral equipment isolation, signal processing, and frequency conversion amplification and switching. In summary, the primary purpose is to provide systems intra and interface compatibility. Changes in other elements of the combat and Interior Communication (IC) systems will frequently mandate either conjunctive modification to switchboards via ship change documents (SCDs), ordnance alteration (ORDALT)/field changes (FCs) or partial or complete replacement of existing switchboards. Typical switchboard mods include hardware/field change kits, ORDALT/SCD/FC instructions, technical manual updates and revisions to other supporting documentation. Hull unique switchboard configurations require hull unique documentation. Subsequent alterations to these switchboards require hull unique design, hardware, installation, and checkout procedures. New Switchboards are normally installed during a regular overhaul by a shipyard. Command and control switchboards are currently installed on and are required for almost all surface combatants and amphibious warfare ships. Individual switchboard unit cost varies from ship to ship, depending upon size, complexity, and whether analog or digital interfaces or some combination thereof are utilized. Modifications to existing switchboards via Ship Alterations (SHIPALTs), SCDs, ORDALTs or FCs are quantified by kits or change packages rather than individual units. The number of kits required for different classes of ships are as follows: DDGs/CGs require three to four (3 - 4) per ship, LSDs require two (2) per ship, LPDs require one (1) per ship, MCMs require (3) per ship and LHDs require two (2) per ship. The magnitude of modifications also varies, as Cruiser Modernization is considerably more complex than the Amphibious Class hulls. Switchboard hardware is normally procured by the Invitation For Bids (IFB) process, from manufacturers on Qualified Products List (QPL)-17000. There are currently six companies listed on QPL-17000. All contracts awarded are competitive, fixed price. llm.acquisitionStrategy: Switchboard hardware is normally procured by the Invitation For Bids (IFB) process from manufacturers on Qualified Products List (QPL)-17000 (six companies currently listed); all contracts awarded are competitive, fixed price.

pes.description: Machinery Control System (MCS) will replace the existing obsolete Versa Module Europa (VME) server with Windows XP operating system (O/S) as part of the ship construction award for LHD8 and LHA6. Both the hardware and software are no longer supported by industry and require a complete replacement. MCS will leverage existing infrastructure replacing internal hardware to the existing system's servers. LHD8, LHA 6-7 will receive a Versatile Performance Switching (VPX) server with Windows 10, or future O/S that provides improved bandwidth for control of the ship's 37 vital engineering systems, while maintain margin for new capabilities to be introduced. The new system provides room for growth and flexibility to easily incorporate emerging cyber security requirements that will help prevent adversarial threats. LI 0933 - LHA/LHD Midlife UNCLASSIFIED Volume 1 - 229 Navy Page 5 of 53 P-1 Line #8 Description: Power Management Platform (PMP) modernization converts legacy analog controls to a digital automated control system. This system gathers and combines all Electric plant data that can be monitored at different control stations throughout the engineering plant ensuring redundancy of the system. PMP simplifies multiple control sequences into single step operations, making possible new control capabilities that were too cumbersome for operators to perform. PMP implements a gradual Ship Service Turbine Generator (SSTG) turbine startup/shutdown sequence which allows the turbine to achieve stabilized temperatures more consistently, reducing operational stress on components and improves reliability and operational availability of the system. PMP automation will reduce electrical system transients and stress on breaker components by employing a Zero Power Transfer (ZPT) strategy, which limits the current flow through an individual breaker to zero during open/close evolutions. During PMP installation obsolete switchboard breakers will be replaced with Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) Whipp and Bourne circuit breakers that will improve navy total ownership by increasing commonality across the fleet and reducing preventative and corrective maintenance. LI 0933 - LHA/LHD Midlife UNCLASSIFIED Volume 1 - 232 Navy Page 8 of 53 P-1 Line #8 The Brushless Generator replacement will reduce down time, total ownership costs, and maintenance costs associated with antiquated brush type generators. Brushless Generator Upgrade replaces five (5) brush-type Ship's Service Turbine Generators on LHDs that are plagued by severe reliability, maintenance and obsolescence problems. Brushless Generator Upgrade will reduce both Ship's Force and depot level maintenance requirements and increase the electric plant Operational Availability (Ao) on LHD class ships. This line funds procurement and installation of VACL Acoustic Superiority machinery modifications. The second component of the AS program, the LVA sonar, is funded under Line Item 2150. The SSN Class Component Upgrades sub-line provides for equipment technical refresh and upgrades that consist of hardware, software, system engineering, integrated logistics support, system test and evaluation, training, data, alteration installation teams and program management. The majority of these upgrades address obsolescence issues that result in unsupportable hardware or provide for improved reliability of systems that have proven to have inadequate reliability in service. The Facilities/Lab Upgrades sub-line procures equipment and material used to implement, sustain and modernize the military high priority Submarine Signature Programs. These spares procurements, technical refreshes and equipment upgrades are key to measuring submarine signatures and sustaining Fleet stealth. These ranges and measurement systems are not funded by other NAVSEA program offices. The program supports all classes of nuclear submarine (SSN/SSBN/SSGN), and associated land-based laboratories/facilities. The Weapons Handling Systems sub-line fund modifications and improvements to SSN 688, SSN 774 and SSN 21 class submarine weapons launching systems, stowage and shipping systems, torpedo tube system components and torpedo tube test equipment. pes.title: LCS Class Support Equipment
pes.description: The Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) Class Support Equipment line procures long-lead major end items and the connective equipment necessary to ensure fit and function required for repairs, and associated engineering, technical, and transportation support services for both LCS variants, Freedom and Independence. The items procured increase availability of vital Fleet assets by reducing repair part procurement and delivery times. LN001 - LCS Spares This line procures shore-based LCS Class Support Equipment (Spares), ensuring their availability in the event of a failure or major casualty to key ship systems. Spares are major end items available on an as need basis to meet Fleet requirements. Inventory objectives are determined by Reliability, Maintainability, and Availability (RM&A) data, the critical application of equipment, and input from the LCS technical community. LN002 - LCS Water Jet Spares This line procures LCS Water Jets and associated propulsion components for both LCS variants. The configurations vary between ships; there are five Water Jet configurations. Water Jet assemblies are designated as Battle Spares and support a rotatable pool for life cycle sustainment. LN003 - Engineering Services This line funds engineering, technical and transportation support for LCS Class Support Equipment. Services include the establishment of Technical Data Packages (TDPs), the creation of associated depot level repair parts lists/installation requirements, and transportation services. LN006 - LCS Ships Class Ancillary Equipment This funding procures the connective equipment necessary to ensure fit and function of procured LCS Class Support Equipment (Spares) when installed. pes.title: Submarine Batteries
pes.description: This program procures replacement of Valve Regulated Lead Acid (VRLA) batteries for all classes of submarines (LOS ANGELES, SEAWOLF, OHIO SSBN/SSGNs and VIRGINIA) as well as funds and manages the production engineering efforts for the In-Service Engineering Agent (ISEA) at NSWC Crane. FY 2027 funding supports the procurement of replacement Valve Regulated Lead Acid (VRLA) batteries for LOS ANGELES (4); OHIO (5); VIRGINIA (12); and associated production engineering. Submarines utilize a Main Storage Battery that provides an immediately available source of backup power that is vital to maintaining ship and reactor plant safety. Submarines with insufficient battery capacity cannot deploy, use the reactor, or operate at-sea. Batteries have a finite life and are consumables; periodic replacements of the battery are incorporated into the maintenance plan for all submarines and are scheduled to minimize the impact to submarine force operational availability. The present geopolitical environment has necessitated Combatant Commanders placing high demands on the submarine force for strategic deterrence, force protection and especially sensitive ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance) missions. The procurement and maintaining of submarine batteries is a pillar that keeps the fleet ready to meet operational commitments. Yearly battery procurement costs are based on fixed, per-cell costs defined by a multi-year Firm Fixed Price contract in effect from FY23-FY28. The quantity of cells required and mix of cell types varies yearly as a function of fleet requirements; consequently, overall battery procurement cost varies despite fixed baseline cell pricing. HM002, HM008, HM009, and HM010 reflect the battery procurement quantities and costs for LOS ANGELES, OHIO, SEAWOLF, and VIRGINIA class submarines respectively. Yearly procurement quantities are projected from the expected average service life of historical batteries. Funding supports procurement the average replacement requirement of 20 battery ship sets each year, though individual yearly quantity varies based on fleet operational requirements. The budget lines also procure battery installation tray sets that are required for all installed batteries. Tray sets are procured during conversion and new construction but must be removed, inspected, and reinstalled during shipboard battery replacement. Procurement of additional shipsets greatly improves battery replacement logistics, enabling schedule flexibility and quick adaption to fleet timelines. pes.title: DDG 1000 Class Support Equipment
pes.description: DDG 1000, a multi-mission surface combatant, will serve as a versatile asset in the context of future Naval Strategy. Armed with an array of weapons, DDG 1000 will provide the Joint Force Commander with precision strike and volume fires. Designed with sustainable payload, multi-spectral stealth and optimal manning, DDG 1000 will take the fight to the enemy with unprecedented striking power. The program is continuing to integrate the Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) weapons system onto the Zumwalt class. CPS integration is a top CNO priority that enhances the Navy's lethality by providing a critical hypersonic attack capability to prevail in Great Power competition. This naval surface hypersonic strike capability will allow the Zumwalt class to conduct independent forward deployed operations and prosecute deep-inland, time-critical, soft and medium-hardened targets in a contested environment. Additionally, when combined with the low observable characteristics of the Zumwalt platform, CPS enhances a uniquely lethal and survivable naval surface platform. The Zumwalt Class will enhance U.S. conventional power projection by providing an independent forward deployed strike platform, with longer range, shorter time of flight, and higher survivability against enemy defenses compared to current capabilities. The Navy will integrate CPS into USS Zumwalt (DDG 1000) and USS Michael Monsoor (DDG 1001) during Building Yard Modernization Periods (BYMP) instead of traditional Docking Selected Restricted Availabilities (DSRA). This shipyard period type maximizes learning and efficiency in order to speed the capability to the fleet. The program will integrate CPS into Lyndon B. Johnson (DDG 1002) during new construction, prior to the ship's arrival in homeport and prior to installation of CPS on DDG 1001. Full CPS operational capability on Zumwalt Class is achieved once CPS is installed in all three ships and they are turned over for Fleet operations. DDG 1000 and DDG 1001 are commissioned ships and the CPS installations for these ships is budgeted with Other Procurement, Navy (OPN) funding. DDG 1002 CPS installation is budgeted in Shipbuilding & Conversion, Navy (SCN) funding. Advanced Payload Modules (APM) are interchangeable end items and are budgeted in OPN. The program provides for DDG 1000 combat system hardware/equipment suite technology refresh to support obsolescence management and address reliability, maintainability & availability (RM&A) issues following fielding. Additionally, the program will sustain and upgrade in-service Zumwalt ships in order to achieve their Expected Service Life (ESL). TRF and Navy IMF are dedicated shore support facilities providing a full range of industrial support. TTF provides realistic training experience in operating and maintaining shipboard equipment for the OHIO Class (SSBN/SSGN) Submarines crews. SSBN/SSGN Submarines operate with two separate crews and TTF is critical in maintaining proficiency and certification for continued at-sea operations when not underway. The magnitude of this funding line is driven by the operational need for modernization and safety alterations. Funding in FY27 supports Strategic Weapons Support Systems (SWSS) Replacement of Hull Keel Depth Transducers for modernization of OHIO Class Hovering and Compensation Systems and modernization of the Missile Dehumidification and Drying Machine. Funding in FY27 also provides additional funding for Passive Fire Protection to wrap Missile Tubes on an additional hull in order to mitigate the potential impact caused by a Missile Compartment Thermal Event. FY27 also funds TRIDENT Load List Range/Depth Additions and Extended Refit Period (ERP) Long Lead Time Material procurements to support SSBN 741's ERP. HM&E Modernization funding enables PMS396 to respond to fleet requests for HM&E modernization for safety and reliability alterations. Funding allows for continued operation and increased supportability of systems, such as Obsolete Equipment Replacement for Ship Control Subsystem upgrades, Life Support Systems upgrades, Torpedo Tube Fiber Optic Interface Upgrade, SSBN TRIDENT Planned Equipment Replacement Program (TRIPER) Obsolescence, SSBN Emergency Diesel Generator (EDG), EDG Rotatable Pool program, and Emergency Diesel Generator Control Panel (DGCP). Funding in this P-1 line also provides funding for Non-Propulsion Electronics Equipment (NPES) that will be installed aboard TRIDENT Class submarines as part of the Obsolete Equipment Replacement (OER) Program. OER Program is the replacement of existing hardware/software that, though functional, has become operationally obsolete, is no longer in production or supportable with spare parts, or has a high failure rate making them no longer cost effective to maintain. OER hardware/software changes are expected to provide significant cost savings via reduced maintenance costs and use Commercial-Off-The-Shelf (COTS) technology wherever possible as long as all technical requirements are met. pes.title: Medium Unmanned Surface Vehicle (MUSVs)
pes.description: The Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel Family of Systems (MUSV FoS) will ensure a suite of USV capability is delivered to the warfighter. There is an Urgent Operational Need (UON) that was validated by the Navy in August 2025 that requires a specific number of MUSVs by FY 2027. The Navy developed the USV Family of Systems (USV FoS) acquisition strategy in early 2026 to provide a comprehensive approach to delivering surface unmanned systems to warfighter at speed and scale. The USV FoS acquisition strategy is aligned to multiple theater priorities and there are urgent demand signals from the Fleet. MUSVs will be designed to employ modular payloads aligned with the CNO's Containerized Capabilities Campaign Plan, enabling the same containers to be fielded across the Fleet on existing platforms to deliver tailored offsets in accordance with the US Navy Fighting Instructions in support of the Golden Fleet initiatives. The MUSV is a foundational element of the Golden Fleet strategy, designed to work in concert with manned warships to increase battlespace awareness and distributed lethality. Central to this concept is the command and control (C2) relationship between manned and unmanned platforms. The program envisions guided-missile frigates (FF(X)) acting as a "quarterback," exercising direct C2 over large flotillas of MUSVs. This allows the frigate to extend its sensor and engagement reach significantly, leveraging the MUSVs as a distributed, forward-deployed extension of its own combat systems. Being a part of the Battleship flexible command-and-control ship set for both manned and unmanned systems, MUSV's can be led in a Surface Action Group, integrate with a Carrier Strike Group, or operate autonomously to secure critical sea lanes. By utilizing RAS C2 through use of Navy warfare system programs of record including BBG(X) Integrated Combat System (ICS), communications systems, and design reservations dedicated to future RAS C2 systems. The MUSV FoS will ensure competitive prototyping produces commercial-based vessel design integrated with platform machinery and autonomy software providing next-generation capabilities that align with Future Surface Combatant Force (FSCF). USV capabilities are being developed incrementally as technologies mature, ensuring efficient and affordable execution. MUSV FoS will focus on improving producibility by being non-exquisite, modular, and expanding competition with multiple vendors. The FY 2027 request for Medium Unmanned Surface Vehicle (MUSVs) includes $121,130 thousand of discretionary to acquire two vehicles and $50,000 thousand of mandatory for one additional vehicle for a total of $171,130 thousand and three vehicles. FY 2027 mandatory funds continue efforts from FY 2026 for continued vehicle procurement. LI 0954 - Medium Unmanned Surface Vehicle (MUSVs) UNCLASSIFIED Volume 1 - 519 Navy Page 1 of 7 P-1 Line #27

pes.title: Deep Subm Sys Proj (DSSP) Equip
pes.description: The Undersea Special Mission Systems Program, formerly Deep Submergence Systems Program (DSSP), is responsible for the procurement, life cycle support, improvement and modernization of assigned platforms and programs. The Undersea Special Missions Systems Program provides for the procurement of equipment to support the establishment and maintenance of fleet capability for a number of programs which perform submarine rescue, escape, search, inspection, and object location and retrieval from the ocean environment. Submarine escape and rescue procurements replace obsolete, non-supportable equipment and subsystems through phased improvement and modernization projects. These projects may include special ship alterations, field change kits, and design corrections. FY2027 funding provides modernization of special mission systems, including the Navy's only Submarine Rescue System (SRS) assets. Modernization of the SRS is necessary to address known reliability and obsolescence issues and to sustain the system through its end-of-life period, ensuring continued operability until replacement. SOURCES: The sources for these acquisitions are limited. There are few private companies actively engaged in deep ocean engineering and even fewer with the specialized certifications, experience, knowledge, and facilities to meet the exacting requirements of submarine escape and rescue. Accordingly, sole source contracts are sometimes required; however, where possible, contracting via open competition is utilized. [P40A / HJ030 - RESCUE SUPPORT EQUIPMENT]: Intervention Systems (Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROV)/ SRS: Intervention assets (ROV) are required to support the SRS world-wide rescue capability mission. Intervention assets are used to clear disabled submarine's seating surfaces, attach salvage fittings, deliver emergency life support stores, and assess distressed submarines condition. The ROV is an unmanned system that reduces operational risk from the previous Intervention Assets that were a manned system, Atmospheric Diving System (ADS). SRS is the pressurized rescue ready system for the U.S. Navy. SRS was delivered in increments; the Submarine Rescue System-Rescue Capable System (SRS-RCS) completed OPEVAL in FY08, and the final component of SRS was the Submarine Rescue System- Submarine Decompression System (SRS-SDS) providing the Transfer Under Pressure (TUP) capability which has been delivered and completed Initial Operating Capability (IOC)/Final Operating Capability (FOC) in FY2019. pes.title: Small Unmanned Surface Vehicles
pes.description: This Other Procurement, Navy line item supports the Golden Fleet Strategy by rapidly fielding many resilient, aeratable systems with diverse capabilities such as the key programs within the Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) Family of Systems (FoS). The sUSV Portfolio consists of a family of systems designed to meet an urgent Geographic Combatant Command Requirement. The sUSV FoS fulfill's the Navy's emergent need to operate sUSVs with autonomous software while operating at long distances. The Navy defined the emergent need to operate and refine tactics with the sUSVs through two efforts. A single sUSV within the sUSV FoS consists of a USV, a communications system, a command and control (C2) station, the procurement and integration of autonomy software, and a payload that will be integrated once the USV is delivered. The GARC is an unmanned vehicle that requires a high bandwidth datalink to operate at long distances. Additionally, the platform is equipped with a radar, infrared devices, and capable of carrying various payloads. The platform includes an autonomy ready package, high-definition surveillance cameras, and remote command and control capabilities. The CORSAIR program consists of a combination of sUSVs that will be used to conduct Naval operations to meet an urgent Geographic Combatant Command Requirement. sUSV CORSAIR is a production-ready, inexpensive Maritime capability leveraging the best of commercial technology and innovations at speed and scale. The One Way Attack (OWA) Surface program consists of sUSVs that will be used to conduct Naval operations to meet an urgent Geographic Combatant Command Requirement. Which is a production-ready, low-cost Maritime capability leveraging the best of commercial and government technology and innovations at speed and scale. Starting in FY2026, LI 0956 has been established for Small Unmanned Surface Vehicles. The Small Unmanned Surface Vehicle Family of Systems was previously funded under LI 1210 H00014. The FY2026 spend plan for 0956 Small Unmanned Surface Vehicles (sUSV) includes $0 million of discretionary and $1,406 million of mandatory for a total of $1,406 million. pes.title: LCAC
pes.description: The LCAC (Landing Craft, Air Cushion), which consists of both the legacy and LCAC 100 classes of craft, mission is to transport weapons systems, equipment, cargo, and personnel of the assault elements for the Marine Air/Ground Task Force from ship to shore and across the beach. The LCAC rides on a cushion of air contained in a flexible skirt and is propelled by two aft-mounted, reversible, variable pitch propellers. It is capable of speeds in excess of 40 knots. The LCAC sustainment funding is programmed for equipment procurement using OPN to replace selected engines, Personnel Transport Modules and other equipment that the fleet urgently requires to maintain acceptable levels of readiness. LC001 - LCAC SYSTEM UPGRADES The LCAC System Upgrade Program provides procurement and installation of components required to maintain acceptable levels of fleet operational readiness. LCAC System Upgrade Program will also provide materials to support systems upgrades. Equipment removal and installation will take place at Assault Craft Unit FOUR (ACU 4), ACU 5 and Naval Beach Unit SEVEN (NBU 7). Specific items procured vary from year to year based on Fleet needs; these items include but are not limited to C4N upgrades and deep skirt replacements. LC002 - ENGINES The ETF-40B engines are enhanced versions of the current TF-40B engines and are installed on Service Life Extension Program (SLEP) craft. Catastrophic engine failures have highlighted the need for spare engines to reduce operational downtime. Engine procurements are also for Pack Up Kits (PUKs) that accompany fleet deployment of LCACs aboard amphibious ships. Additional ETF-40B Engines will be needed to meet operational needs. LC007 - LIGHTWEIGHT ARMOR The portable lightweight armor system replaces the existing armor system. The portable system can be transported via a Container Express (CONEX) box and provides the fleet ballistic/fragmentation protection to manned spaces on the craft as well as to selected machinery components. LC008 - COLD WEATHER KITS LCAC requires to be capable of operating in temperature ranges from 10 degrees Fahrenheit to 100 degrees Fahrenheit. In order to operate in weather conditions below 50 degrees Fahrenheit, a cold weather kit is required. Snow and ice accumulation leads to actuation of a safety system that bypasses the main engine inlet air filtration system and allows engines to draw in unfiltered air. Cold weather kits prevent snow and ice accumulation in the main engines during cold weather operations keeping the craft operational during deployments. pes.title: Underwater EOD Equipment
pes.description: Underwater Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) program supplies EOD and maritime expeditionary forces with the necessary allowance outfitting, and diving and diving-related equipment aligned to fulfill assigned missions that includes Expeditionary Mine Countermeasures (ExMCM), and other maritime expeditionary missions. Most equipment must have inherently low acoustic and magnetic signatures to support maritime operations in the vicinity of influence fired ordnance. This funding supports outfitting the Navy's only comprehensive capability that can conduct full spectrum detect-to-engage ExMCM missions. Specifically, the (EOD) program supports EOD units worldwide as well as Mobile Diving and Salvage Units (MDSUs) and Naval Construction Forces (NCF) across the globe. The nature of the missions assigned to EOD and MCM forces under OPNAVINST 3501.97, Required Operational Capabilities & Projected Operational Environments (ROC/POE), require an aggregated set of systems and equipment to perform the wide range of mine countermeasures, underwater detection, location, investigation, force protection, exploitation, and neutralization tasks that comprise the mission set. The requirements for the procurement of each of these system suites are articulated in OPNAV approved requirements documents in accordance with DoD Directive 5000.2 and SECNAVINST 5000.2, and in accordance with the approved ExMCM ICD and ExMCM Concept of Operations. pes.description: This budget provides for "S" cognizance (Shipboard, Hull, Mechanical & Electrical (HM&E) equipment for surface ships and aircraft carriers) which are not in any specific category. This equipment accomplishes program alterations for installation during CNO and Fleet availabilities, fills Fleet requisitions from casualties and attrition, provide tech refresh upgrades, and replaces obsolete equipment. Primary objectives are to maintain or improve readiness, safety, reliability, reduce workload, lower maintenance costs, improve sailor quality of life, and/or sustain ship classes through their notional life or beyond. The budget purchases and installs various equipment including machinery pumps, generators, ship propellers and shafts, air compressors, davits, A/C Plants, and steam propulsion items. It also procures allowance items as required by the Coordinated Shipboard Allowance List (COSAL). Major programs are the CVN Class Machinery Plant Upgrades, MACHALTs, CVN Cybersecurity, and CVN 78 class upgrades. [P40A / LT060 - MACHALTs]: The Machinery Alteration (MACHALT) Program supports identification, procurement, and installation of Hull, Mechanical and Electrical (HM&E) internal equipment and system improvements on in-service surface ships. MACHALTs are installed via the Navy Modernization Process (NMP) in the following priority order: (1) Mandatory Safety/Statutory, (2) Component-level installations targeting risk to TYCOM operational redlines, (3) Safety, (4) Readiness, Maintainability and Availability, and (5) Obsolescence Alts. pes.title: Ship Maintenance, Repair and Modernization
pes.description: Division A of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020, Public Law 116-93 appropriated funding in Other Procurement, Navy (OPN) to initiate a program funding private contracted ship maintenance in the U.S. Pacific Fleet (CPF) in Fiscal Year (FY) 2020. Division C of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 continued this program in the U.S. Pacific Fleet, and Division C of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022 expanded the program to include both U.S. Pacific Fleet and U.S. Fleet Forces (FFC). FY 2027 funds $2.7B for Continental United Status (CONUS) private contracted surface and submarine maintenance in both U.S. Pacific Fleet (CPF) and U.S. Fleet Forces Command (FFC). Funding private contracted ship maintenance planned for CPF and FFC with OPN allows the Navy to implement commercial best practices for ship maintenance and achieve Navy's A-120 contracting policy. It provides more flexibility to extend contract lead times, enables the Navy to address emergent repair requirements, and strengthens industry partnerships. The program continues to provide stability and financial efficiency to its industry partners, and continues the more stringent fiscal discipline demonstrated in the execution of the program. The Navy remains committed and motivated to utilizing this program to improve both the execution of depot-level maintenance and the overall readiness posture of the U.S. Navy's maritime forces. pes.title: Diving and Salvage Equipment
pes.description: DIVING AND SALVAGE EQUIPMENT: The equipment procured from this Diving and Salvage OPN line item provides critical diving and salvage equipment that enables planned/emergent waterborne submarine/ship repairs, salvage and battle damage repair operations, search and recovery to water depths up to 20,000 feet of seawater and Undersea Clandestine Insertion of Special Operations Forces (UCI-SOF) (service common equipment) to keep our Navy fleet operational and enable national priority missions. Program objectives are to: (1) provide increased safety for divers, (2) increase underwater ship maintenance capabilities, (3) provide reliable, rapid response salvage capability, and (4) reduce diving equipment maintenance costs by standardizing configuration of diving systems in the Fleet. FY-27 investment in Diving capability continues to emphasize phased replacement of aging life support equipment including surface-supplied diving helmet upgrades, HP composite flask replacements, SCUBA regulators and surface supplied augmented SCUBA sets, an HP Air Compressor, Air Rack Upgrades, Multi-occupant flexible recompression chamber and a Diver Launch and Recovery System. Navy dive computers, required by each diver to calculate decompression penalties, will also be procured. This equipment is essential to maintaining diving readiness throughout the Fleet. Additionally, we will make investments in new technology equipment that offer capability gains such as Diver Augmented Visual Display (DAVD) 3-D Sonar. These systems will produce a virtual environment in which a diver can operate and be directed by topside supervisors to execute salvage, search and recovery and other missions. Lastly, we continue to invest in upgrades to the Navy Experimental Diving Unit, which houses national assets such as the Ocean Simulation Facility (OSF). The OSF is a 40+ year old system that permits advanced research and testing of diving technology, diving procedures, human performance, decompression and physiology essential to advancing diving capabilities. FY-27 investment in Salvage includes a salvage firefighting kit, Deep Drone Upgrade, Lighting Kits, Kerrie Cable Underwater Cutting System, Salvage BDR Material Kit, Salvage Roller Bags, a Full Ocean Depth Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) and a Full Ocean Depth Line Spooler; all will be used for ship salvage. In Underwater Ship Husbandry (UWSH) we continue investments in cofferdam systems (4 standard and 1 complex), surface ship support systems, video/camera equipment, UWSH Storage and Shipping Containers, a pier-side support van, a propeller system repair kit, power tools, rigging systems, and a submarine support system. Underwater Ship Husbandry investments continue to produce significant returns on investment by eliminating the need for emergent dry dockings, thereby returning ships to service faster and less expensive than traditional shipyard availabilities. pes.title: Operating Forces IPE
pes.description: The Operating Forces Industrial Plant Equipment (IPE) budget provides funding for capital equipment procurement in support of naval shipyards and Fleet I-level maintenance activities. These investments deliver modern, innovative equipment essential for maintaining submarines, aircraft carriers, and surface ships; and reducing dependence on outdated IPE, weight handling systems, and nuclear support infrastructure. By modernizing equipment infrastructure, these procurements enhance maintenance productivity and throughput, reduce costly rework, and help maintain cost and schedule performance across submarine, aircraft carrier, and surface ship availabilities. The Capital Investment Program (CIP), a component of the Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program (SIOP), supports capital equipment modernization efforts at the four public naval shipyards and their detachments. This includes support for Virginia-Class repairs at Norfolk Naval Shipyard (NNSY), Portsmouth Naval Shipyard (PNSY), Puget Sound Naval Shipyard (PSNS & IMF), and Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard (PHNSY & IMF). CIP includes providing equipment and machinery to increase the capacity of the Navy shipyards to maintain Virgina-class submarines and Ford-class carriers. Additionally, the Fleet Maintenance Investment Program (FMIP) funds capital equipment replacement and modernization at the U.S. Navy's regional maintenance centers and their detachments. Cost Code KN443 supports the Enterprise Remote Monitoring (eRM) system. eRM is the Navy's Condition Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) Program of Record supporting Distance Support, Sea Power 21, Ship Maintenance (SHIPMAIN), CBM and CBM + initiatives. It is a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) based system that reduces Total Ownership Costs (TOC), maintenance and operating costs of monitored equipment by ensuring maintenance is accomplished based upon evidence of need. Condition Based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) is a maintenance optimization program that can generate significant benefits through maintenance program resets, maintenance effectiveness reviews, and active reliability centered maintenance (RCM) strategies at the program level. Employed as an enduring cross-life-cycle maintenance strategy, the program offers a technical solution to reduce maintenance burdens, increase operational availability and mission reliability of monitored systems, assists with identifying enterprise-wide cost avoidance, and will reduce overall life cycle costs. The Integrated Condition Assessment System (ICAS) hardware and software aboard Surface Fleet hulls (FY25 and prior Cost Codes KN800 and KN900) transitioned into the FY26 and out eRM program cited above. The FY 2026 spend plan amount for Other Procurement, Navy includes $394,998 thousand of discretionary and $390,600 thousand of mandatory (reconciliation) for a total of $785,598. pes.title: LCS Common Mission Modules Equipment
pes.description: Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) focused mission packages provide the operational commander with capabilities to perform Mine Countermeasures (MCM) operations, and a Surface Warfare (SUW) detect-to-engage capability to counter small boat threats and aircraft such as drones. A Mission Package (MP) is a combination of warfare Mission Modules (MM) with specialized crew, support equipment, and vehicles, including embarked manned helicopters, unmanned aircraft and maritime systems. MMs are packaged in a modular fashion so that they can be quickly swapped in and out pier side on any LCS platform. The Common Mission Modules Equipment line funds the procurement of MCM and SUW MP support containers and C5I equipment that is common across the mission packages (Mission Package Computing Environment (MPCE), Technology Refresh of the Multi-Vehicle Communications System (MVCS), Mission Package Consoles (MPC) and Training Equipment). MCM and SUW support containers do not comprise a MP and are deployable only as part of a Mission Module (MM). A MM is deployable and capable of meeting its focused mission requirements on a LCS only when it includes the full complement of Common Mission Modules Equipment combined with all the required mission systems. Other Related Budgets: BLIs: OPN 1601, OPN 1602, OPN 1603, OPN 4248, OPN 2622, OPN 2624, WPN 4221, WPN 4225, RDT&E 0603596N, SCN 2127 [P40A / LM008 - MPCE]: Commercial Off The Shelf (COTS)- Based Common Computing environment will support legacy Mission Package (MP) Command & Control (C2) applications and transition to Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) & Navy Open Architecture Computing Environment (OACE). It also provides a common computing environment to support the execution of Mission Package Application Software (MPAS), the shipboard tactical software associated with each mission package that enables execution of its focused mission. Includes installation and checkout on-board the seaframe. In addition, Mission Package Portable Control Stations (MPPCS) are required to support pre-deployment checkouts, to support shore-based and vessels of opportunity operations of mission packages and off-board vehicles. [P40A / MPCE 2.X]: MPCE 2.X improves data extraction, data encryption, cybersecurity enhancements, and virtualization capabilities needed for all Mission Packages (MPs). MPCE 2.X baseline was split to support the evolution of different versions of the LCS. MPCE v2.0 for LCS Lethality and Survivability and MPCE v2.1 for non-Lethality and Survivability hulls. pes.title: LCS MCM Mission Modules
pes.description: The Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) Mine Countermeasures (MCM) Mission Package (MP) counters bottom, tethered, near surface, and surface mines in the littorals without putting Sailors in the minefield. When the MCM MP is embarked, LCS is capable of conducting detect-to-engage operations (hunting, sweeping, and neutralization) against shallow and deep-water sea mine threats. The MCM MP provides these capabilities through the use of sensors and weapons deployed from an embarked MH-60S multi-mission helicopter and unmanned offboard vehicles. MCM MP achieved Initial Operational Capability in 31MAR2023. The embarked MH-60S employs the Organic Airborne Mine Countermeasures (OAMCM) systems to provide rapid and long range airborne detection and neutralization to clear operations in littoral zones, confined straits, choke points, and the Amphibious Operations Area (AOA) quickly. The Airborne Mine Neutralization (AMN) Module (MH-60S Helo + Airborne Mine Neutralization System) and Near Surface Detection (NSD) Module (MH-60S Helo + Airborne Laser Mine Detection System) achieved Initial Operational Capability (IOC) in FY 2017. The Unmanned Minesweeping (UMS) Module is composed of the MCM Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) and Minesweeping Payload Delivery System (PDS) and Towed Acoustic Generator (TAG). The MCM USV and Minesweeping PDS was previously known as Unmanned Influence Sweeping System (UISS) which achieved Milestone C and is currently in Full Rate Initial Production (FRIP). The Remote Minehunting (RMH) Module consists of a PDS and a Towed Sonar which detects and identifies bottom and tethered mines. In FY 2020, the MCM USV established a mature Technical Data Package (TDP) and was used for the award of the Production contract in FY2022. The Unmanned Influence Sweep System (UISS) TDP is mature and is being leveraged to procure Minesweeping PDS in Q1FY2025. In FY 2022, the Minehunting PDS was procured via a sole source delivery order on the Raytheon IDIQ contract. A competitive production contract was awarded for future Minehunting PDS procurements in Q1 FY2025. The Mine Neutralization (MN) module will consist of the MCM USV with a near-surface mine neutralization payload, necessitating future procurement of MN PDSs. The Buried Minehunting (BMH) Module (Knifefish Unmanned Undersea Vehicle) detects and identifies buried mines and mines in a high clutter environment. The program achieved Milestone C in FY 2019 and entered into Low Rate Initial Production (LRIP) for five (5) Block 0 systems in FY 2019. In FY 2021, prime contractor for Knifefish is General Dynamics Mission Systems (GDMS) located in Quincy, MA, was awarded a contract to retrofit the LRIP systems with Block 1 capabilities and upgrade a number of performance characteristics to meet Navy bottom and buried mine hunting requirements. The Navy will conduct a limited validation of these capabilities during system acceptance testing and sell off to the government in Q1-Q3FY24. Upon delivery of these systems

pes.title: LCS SUW Mission Modules
pes.description: The Surface Warfare (SUW) Mission Package (MP) provides Littoral Combat Ships (LCS) with increased firepower and offensive/defensive capabilities against large numbers of small manned and unmanned threats including fast attack craft, fast inshore attack craft, and aircraft, giving LCS the ability to protect the sea lanes and move a force quickly through a choke point or other strategic waterway. The SUW MP is composed of the following modules: Surface-to-Surface Missile Module (SSMM), Gun Mission Module (GMM), Maritime Security Module (MSM), and an Aviation Module. The SSMM provides offensive firepower to engage enemy threats at close range. A recent capability upgrade allows the SSMM to counter aircraft like drones, extending defense in addition to fast attack and fast inshore attack craft. The SSMM is comprised 24 Longbow Hellfire Missiles, 12 MK210 Launchers, and supporting hardware. The GMM augments the ship's 57mm gun with two high-velocity 30mm cannons. The MSM supports the embarkation of Visit, Board, Search, and Seizure (VBSS) teams. The Aviation Module incorporates various unmanned aircraft for surveillance. The GMM, MSM, and initial Aviation Module (with the MH-60R/S) achieved Initial Operational Capability (IOC) in FY 2014. The SSMM achieved IOC in FY 2019. For surveillance, the package aviation component has evolved. Initially, the package was first upgraded with the MQ-8B Fire Scout, a vertical take-off unmanned aerial vehicle (VTUAV) used for finding and identifying surface contacts. In FY24, because of the MQ-8B sunset, the Fleet invested in a contractor owned/contractor operated Aerosonde. The MK 4.7 Aerosonde, a fixed-wing unmanned aircraft that provides long-endurance Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) and is proven reliable for both land and sea operations. In FY26, the ScanEagle unmanned aircraft was added as a compatible asset, allowing it to be interchanged with the Aerosonde based on mission requirements. The inventory objective of ten deployable SUW MP has been delivered to the Fleet. Fleet requirements for SSMM has been met with five (5) production assets. A SUW MP is considered deployable and capable of meeting its mission requirements on an LCS only when it includes the full complement of Common Mission Modules Equipment (Line Item Number 1600) and the mission systems composing the LCS SUW Mission Module (Line Item Number 1603). [P40A / SU001 - GUN MODULE]: The Gun Mission Module (GMM) comprises two high velocity 30mm cannons to augment the ship's 57mm gun, and embarked support aircraft (MH-60R/S helicopter with Hellfire missile) for the detection, identification, and classification of surface contacts. [P40A / Gun Module Modernization/Technology Refresh]: Procures modernized Gun Module Remote Control System (GMRCS) and Gun User Interface Device (GUID), each contain computational equipment (including critical MAGIC-1s and Maintenance Station laptops) that are end-of-life and can no longer be procured.

pes.title: LCS In-Service Modernization
pes.description: Modernization/maintenance efforts support Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) requirements to remain operational and meet mission needs. This line provides funding for ship changes and improvements related to mandatory safety, cyber security remediation, habitability, obsolescence, reliability, command and control, and communication modifications to maintain LCS operational availability and achieve ships' expected service life. Funding covers planned CNO availabilities and two years of planning costs and long lead time materials (LLTM) in advance of CNO availabilities. This line provides funds for the procurement, planning, installation design, and installation for Lethality and Survivability (L&S) modifications for both LCS variants (Independence and Freedom). L&S modifications seek to leverage existing Navy Program of Record systems allowing for more rapid implementation of holistic combat system enhancements. These modifications will improve displays, infrastructure, radar, tactical data link, cybersecurity, and navigation capabilities. L&S introduces commonality between LCS variants and other surface combatants leveraging common source libraries, Total Ship Computing Environment (TSCE), MK-20 Electro-Optical Surveillance System, Surface Electronic Warfare Improvement Program, Nulka, MK-160 Gun Computer System, Data Links (IND only), Mode 5 IFF (IND only) and Navigation systems. The use of Navy Standard systems improves capability, simplifies training, and decreases life cycle costs. MT002 - LCS Class Design Improvements This budget line covers the procurement and installation of a Combat Systems and C4I Condition Based Maintenance (CBM) System, designed to monitor and collect maintenance data then periodically transfer the data ashore via a Virtualized Data Transport System (VDTS) for analysis. The CBM equipment currently monitors performance of SPS-75 and SPS-77 Radars, MK-49 RAM, and MK-110 Gun, but the Program Office is researching the potential for other systems to be monitored. MT003 - LCS Maintenance Modernization This budget line funds back-fit, upgrade, and fact of life obsolescence changes on both Freedom and Independence Variant Littoral Combat Ships. The Modernization construct is split out into 7 categories: Safety; Targeted Performance Enhancement; Obsolescence; Advanced Engineering Control System (AECS); Communication; Hull, Mechanical and Electrical (HM&E); and Navigation. These categories enable improved planning and tracking of ship changes as technology and mission evolve. The scope/requirements for maintenance modernization is dependent on hull availability, applicability, procurement timeline, and ship alteration maturity. llm.acquisitionStrategy: Lethality and Survivability funding procures a common Combat Management System comprised of Government Furnished Equipment (GFE), leveraging existing Navy Program of Record systems for more rapid implementation.

pes.title: LSD Midlife & Modernization
pes.description: Modernized LSD 41/49 Class ships transport and launch amphibious craft and vehicles with their crews and embarked personnel in amphibious assault operations. Supporting amphibious operations include landings via Landing Craft, Air Cushion (LCAC), conventional landing craft, and helicopters, onto hostile shores. [P40A / ST5IN LSD Installation / DSA / AIT]: Planned effort by the Alteration Installation Teams (AITs) and the Design Support Activity (DSA) to address ship's growing obsolescence issues and maintenance intensive areas via support in the Modernization Availabilities. [P40A / Slewing Arm Davit (SLAD) Embarkation Platform Installation]: LSD Class ships require an embarkation platform for loading and unloading of personnel during launch and recovery operations utilizing the new Lake Shore Inc. Slewing Arm Davit (SLAD). The upgrade is required due to limited space in the area of the 11M RIB stowage, which limits the ability of the crew to efficiently load and unload personnel, particularly during recovery operations. [P40A / Slewing Arm Davit (SLAD) Installation]: This SHIPALT replaces the Welin Lambie LUM 12A or Lakeshore Gravity Boat Davit currently installed on LSD 41/49 Class ships, with a new Slewing Arm Davit (SLAD) from Oldenburg Group Inc. The existing systems will be removed and the OGI SLAD will be installed in the same general location of the current systems. The new system is a SLAD design with single point pick up of the boats versus the two points pick up used by the existing systems. [P40A / Ballast Control Console (BCC)]: Provides upgrades to the existing Ballast Control Consoles (BCC) and replaces legacy BCC with a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) based digital, networked system. This mission and safety critical SCD address system degradation due to obsolescence issues, extensive downtime and reduced system capability/reliability. The system is currently operating in a degraded capacity and requires immediate replacement. [P40A / Damage Control Console (DCC)]: This SCD upgrades the existing Damage Control (DC) Console and interior communication sensor monitoring (IC/SM) alarm panels within Damage Control Central on-board ship with a Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) based control system that will provide all current functionality and utilizes the Advanced Engineering Control System (AECS) network backbone. The software will leverage the LSD 47 interface for system screen layout and user interaction but will be developed using the current Platform Independent Machinery Control System (PIMCS) software architecture and includes the Advanced Damage Control System (ADCS) hardware and software. ADCS provides real-time, dynamic ship status and parametric information, and accepts feedback on actions taken by watch standers. pes.title: Small & Medium UUV
pes.description: Lionfish and Viperfish are the next generation UUVs that will replace the MK18 Mod 1 and Mod 2 UUVs currently in the fleet. They are the Navy's first cybersecure UUVs, which support mine countermeasures (MCM), Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment (IPOE), Subsea and Seabed Warfare (SSW), Naval Special Warfare (NSW) Maritime Homeland Defense (MHLD) and combat salvage. Both provide a critical Detect-to-Engage capability to Expeditionary Mine counter measures (ExMCM) forces, organized into 18 ExMCM companies across the Navy. These UUVs can be used in very shallow to deep waters to clear sea mines and enable fleet movement and maneuver through chokepoints and key water space, enable logistics at sea and between sea and shore in a contested environment, and to enable movement of Marines from ship to shore to seize and hold key terrain in support of Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations. P5 / 5N300 Lionfish is a Small Unmanned Undersea Vehicle (SUUV) that replaces the legacy MK 18 Mod 1, utilizes advanced sensors and autonomy, and can be launched and recovered from small boats and craft, surface ships, vessels of opportunity, submarines, piers and shorelines, and various platforms. Viperfish, the deep water variant of Lionfish, replaces legacy MK 18 Mod 2 UUVs, and leverages recent innovation and technical advances to enable it to be delivered in a Small UUV form factor using Lionfish as a baseline as an ECP with enhanced depth performance and mission capability. P5 / 5N001 KNIFEFISH (SMCM UUV w/LFBB)]: The Knifefish Surface Mine Countermeasure Unmanned Undersea Vehicle (SMCM UUV) program procures Unmanned Undersea Vehicles to support clandestine mine detection capability against volume and bottom mines including buried mine detection. The Knifefish system is composed of two UUVs, batteries, launch and handling system, and other support equipment. P5 / 5N100 TETRA: TETRA is a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) with the capacity for multiple mission payloads as a key enabler to Subsea and Seabed Warfare (SSW) as identified in the SSW Initial Capabilities Document (ICD). A single TETRA system is comprised of 2 ROVs equipped with mission-dependent payload(s) and Ancillary Equipment The FY 2026 spend plan for Small and Medium Unmanned Undersea Vehicles (UUVs) program includes $7,000 thousand of discretionary funding and $345,086 thousand of mandatory funding for a total of $352,086 thousand. The mandatory funds unmanned underwater vehicle production. The Knifefish system is composed of two UUVs, batteries, launch and handling system, and other support equipment. pes.title: Large UUV
pes.description: The Dragonfish Large Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (LUUV) addresses a priority Fleet requirement for a below-water Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) task with classification of targets of interest and activation of a purpose-built payload. The system consists of a vehicle, a payload, and a support system. The Dragonfish LUUV is the result of a Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) Commercial Solutions Opening (CSO) that assessed commercially available LUUVs. Dragonfish provides the ability to have a dispersed, long range, persistent underwater sensing and payload delivery platform to use in a contested environment. The platform will be large diameter, scalable, low-cost autonomous unmanned system with persistent reach and payload capacity to conduct desired mission sets. pes.title: Extra Large UUV
pes.description: The Combat Autonomous Maritime Platform (CAMP) Extra Large Unmanned Undersea Vehicle (XLUUV) is a Navy's Extra Large UUV effort as part of the Family of UUVs. U.S. adversaries continue to develop asymmetric capabilities and capacities to deter, disrupt, or delay the entry of U.S. and allied naval forces, and pose a constant challenge as the Maritime Strategy is implemented. Evolving submarine technologies offer enhanced stealth, speed, endurance, weapons, and operational proficiency, trends foretelling that the adversary submarine of the future will have a significantly larger sphere of influence, while presenting less vulnerability to ASW forces. The effective offensive engagement range of the adversary submarine of the future will continue to match or outrange individual U.S. and multinational platform sensors and weapons in many tactical environments. Submarines are an increasing threat to all Naval and Allied ships, particularly modern diesel and state-of-the-art nuclear submarines, and faster, more accurate torpedoes. Not only can the presence of potential hostile submarines delay naval combatant action until they are located and neutralized, submarines can also disrupt all seaborne logistics supply for any ground campaign as well as maritime commerce. pes.description: MISSION DESCRIPTION AND BUDGET ITEM JUSTIFICATION: This program procures submarine systems and equipment for installation on all classes of submarines to maintain clear acoustical, tactical, and operational superiority over submarine and surface combatants in all scenarios through detection, classification, localization, and contact following. Future procurements, detailed below, are focused on supporting Littoral Warfare, Regional Sea Denial, Strike Group Support, Diesel Submarine Detection, Surveillance, and Peacetime Engagement. A-RCI is a multi-phased, evolutionary development effort geared toward addressing acoustic superiority issues through the rapid introduction of interim products applicable to SSN 688, 688I Flight, SSN21, SSGN, VIRGINIA Class, and OHIO Class Submarines. A-RCI Phase II provided towed array processing improvements; A-RCI Phase III provides spherical array processing improvements, and A-RCI Phase IV provides AN/BSY-1 High Frequency Upgrades for SSN 688I, SSGN, and SEAWOLF Classes. As part of Navy's plan to maintain acoustic superiority for in-service submarines, reduce obsolescence, and provide increased capability, the A-RCI program will modernize and sustain approximately 8-12 SSNs and 2-3 SSBNs per year through executing bi-annual software Advanced Processing Builds (APBs) and bi-annual hardware Technical Insertions (TIs). Towed Array Refurbishment & Reliability Upgrades sustain current in-service TB-16/34 Fatline and TB-23/29A Thinline towed arrays. Towed System procurements provide upgrade/support for OK-276, OK-634, OK-542 and OA-9070 Series Towed Array Handlers installed on SSN688, SSN 688I, SSN21, SSGN, VIRGINIA Class, and OHIO Class Submarines. pes.title: SURTASS
pes.description: PROGRAM COVERAGE: Surveillance Towed Array Sensor System (SURTASS) is the mobile, tactical, and strategic arm of the Navy's undersea surveillance capability that provides deep ocean and littoral acoustic detection and cueing for tactical weapon platforms against diesel and nuclear submarines as well as surface vessels in any given Area of Operations worldwide. Dedicated Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) T-AGOS ships tow long acoustic arrays that collect acoustic data and relay that data to shore facilities via satellites for processing and fusion of the resulting contact data with other sensors. Currently, there are five Small Waterplane Area Twin Hull (SWATH) Passive (P)/Active (A) T-AGOS ships operating in the Pacific area. Ship configurations are: T-AGOS 22 USNS LOYAL (1), a SWATH-P platform which supports passive operations using the TB-29A Twinline (TL-29A) array, providing improved detection and classification capability. This ship class uses the Integrated Common Processor (ICP) signal processing and display system common with the SSN Acoustic Rapid Commercial Off the Shelf (COTS) Insertion (ARCI) Sonar Processing System. Three (3) T-AGOS SWATH-P platforms, T-AGOS 19 USNS VICTORIOUS, T-AGOS 20 USNS ABLE, and T-AGOS 21 USNS EFFECTIVE, supporting passive/active operations, configured with the ICP processing and display system, the TL-29A array, and the Compact Low Frequency Active (CLFA) transmit capability. One (1) Low Frequency Active (LFA) equipped ship, T-AGOS 23 USNS IMPECCABLE, a SWATH-A platform configured with the ICP processing and display system, the TL-29A array, and the Low Frequency Active (LFA) transmit capability. The active capability provides greatly improved detection against diesel submarines as well as the quiet nuclear submarine threat. In addition to the five platforms described above, two (2) shore sites are configured with the ICP processing and display suites to receive the T-AGOS acoustic data via Super High Frequency (SHF) satellite communication links. One of the two shore sites is equipped with three (3) SURTASS Team Trainers (STTs) to support Home Port Training Periods. A cost sharing agreement with Japan also provides two (2) shore sites and four (4) Japanese SWATH ships with similar capability to the T-AGOS SWATH-P ships for the Western Pacific region. Funding supports the U.S. cost share for the procurement of Towed Arrays for the new J-AOS-4 ship. The Expeditionary Surveillance Towed Array Sensor System (SURTASS-E) provides a SURTASS passive capability packaged in ISO-Vans (ISO-International Organization for Standardization) for mobilization on Vessels of Opportunity (VOOs). It was developed as a Rapid Prototyping, Experimentation, and Demonstration (RPED) project, tasked to re-package, test, and demonstrate an expeditionary variant of the passive component of the SURTASS acoustic surveillance system that can be used as a surrogate for some of the SURTASS capabilities provided by traditional T-AGOS class vessels.

llm.acquisitionStrategy: Funding supports the U.S. cost share under a cost sharing agreement with Japan for procurement of towed arrays for the new J-AOS-4 ship; systems use COTS-based ICP processing common with the SSN ARCI sonar system.
llm.summary: Procures Surveillance Towed Array Sensor System (SURTASS) equipment for T-AGOS ships, shore sites, and the expeditionary SURTASS-E variant providing undersea acoustic surveillance.

pes.title: Maritime Battlespace Awareness
pes.description: Funding for LI 2900 Maritime Integrated Broadcast Service (MIBS) has been realigned into LI 2361 Automatic Identification System (AIS) as part of Other Procurement, Navy Line Item-Consolidation starting in FY 2026. This effort consolidates the existing number of PEs/BLIs identified by BSOs and FMB to group technology projects to allow flexibility that would foster innovation and promote efficiency. PE/BLI consolidation meets the DoW Implementation Plan from the Commission on PPBE Interim Report. 1U030: AIS is required for safety of navigation for all surface ships and submarines. AIS is a maritime Very High Frequency (VHF) communication system, which allows ships to exchange navigation, ship identification, and cargo information machine-to-machine via VHF transponders. AIS provides vessels with the ability to rapidly identify and track commercial shipping, which significantly increases the Navy's ability to distinguish between normal and suspicious merchant ships headed towards United States and allied ports around the globe. AIS provides critical track data to the Common Operational Picture (COP) on surface ships, AN/BYG-1 Combat System on submarines, Global Command and Control System-Maritime (GCCS-M) on Force Level ships, and Global Command and Control System-Joint (GCCS-J) at Fleet Maritime Operations Centers (MOC). The AIS submarine configuration provides an interface to the AN/BYG-1 Combat System and encrypted AIS capability. This capability dramatically improves the Combatant Commanders' situational awareness and Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) data sharing capabilities in support of regional engagement and tracking efforts against potential maritime terrorism threats. Funds will be used to continue the initial fielding of AIS (V)9 Program of Record systems, their follow-on cyber hardening upgrades, as well as the continuation of surface ship cyber hardening. The AIS submarine variant consists of a combination of government/commercial software, AIS power and navigation subsystem, AIS antenna selector switch, AIS antenna interface unit, AIS data distribution laptop, and AIS terminal data processing unit. The need for AIS systems is especially important for submarines, which have limited maneuverability. The AIS (V)3 and (V)9 Submarine configuration provides situational awareness (to include encrypted AIS message traffic from United States Coast Guard vessels) during time-constrained ascents to communications depth, thereby significantly reducing the risk of a collision. In order to address potential vulnerabilities identified by the Naval Cyber Warfare Development Group (NCWDG) and in compliance with the "Expression of Cyber Requirement for Automatic Identification System" dated 31 Jan 2017, a cybersecurity engineering change will be implemented on all AIS systems in order to protect downstream systems from malformed or anomalous AIS data. Funds are being used to procure and install a new Warship AIS compliant transponder and AIS Terminal B
